title: Simulated Ultrasound for Robotic Femoral Access
summary: A GPU physics simulation of a probe pressing a femoral leg, with the ultrasound image rendered live, as a training ground for autonomous femoral vascular access.
body: In emergency medicine and resuscitation, clinicians often need fast access to the common femoral vein and artery. Ultrasound shows both vessels, and pressing the probe tells them apart: the thin-walled vein collapses while the artery holds its shape. A robot doing this on its own has to learn that cue. Its probe deforms the tissue, which in turn changes the image it uses to decide its next move.

This project builds a simulator fast enough for that loop. Running on a single GPU in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, it models the leg as soft tissue, presses it with a virtual probe, and ray-traces the ultrasound image of the deforming anatomy at about 18 frames per second. The settings were tuned to cut the solver's time per frame by a factor of almost 1,000 while staying within about one percentage point of the finest reference simulation.

The model was validated against a benchtop phantom pressed by a robot arm. It predicted the artery's cross-section within 5 percentage points at every depth and matched the vein closely through the first part of the press. Seeded with literature tissue properties, the full leg model reproduces the clinical signal: the vein collapses well before the artery.
